extracted.intended_audience: performers, theatre students, improv practitioners, and general readers interested in improvisational theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for performing and producing improvised theatre (both comedic and non-comedic), covering technique, format (shortform/longform), ensemble behavior, and stagecraft. Useful for performers, teachers, and troupe directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer and acceptance (the 'Yes, and...' rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: With each spoken word or action an improviser makes an offer defining some element of the reality of the scene; it is the responsibility of the other improvisers to accept the offers. Accepting an offer is usually accompanied by adding a new offer; this process is referred to as 'Yes, and...' and is considered the cornerstone of improvisational technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Yes, and...' rule applies especially in a scene's early stage to establish a shared base reality; once the base is set, performers can use 'if (this is true), then (what else can also be true)' to progress the scene into comedy (per Upright Citizens Brigade manual). Acceptance builds the scene collaboratively; refusal prevents development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment / making concrete offers
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer can include giving another character a name, identifying a relationship, a location, or using mime to define the physical environment. These activities are also known as endowment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endowment anchors the scene's reality for fellow improvisers; examples: naming a character, assigning relationships or props via mime. Viola Spolin developed techniques (theatre games) that formalize making useful offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blocking/negation (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: To not accept an offer is known as blocking, negation, or denial, which usually prevents the scene from developing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some performers may deliberately block or break character for comedic effect (known as gagging), but this generally prevents the scene from advancing and is frowned upon by many improvisers. Blocking is cited as a major cause of stalled scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect continuity and validity of the imaginary environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers are encouraged to respect the validity and continuity of the imaginary environment defined by themselves and their fellow performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care not to contradict established physical or narrative facts (e.g., don't walk through an imaginary table; don't miraculously survive repeated bullet wounds). Maintaining internal consistency preserves believability and allows scenes to develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mime / 'space object' work instead of physical props
rubrics_metrics.description: Many improvisers eschew physical props in favor of mime; this technique is commonly known as 'space object work' or 'space work' rather than 'mime'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improv companies may nevertheless keep some readily accessible props for use, but relying on space object work preserves flexibility and the infinite possibilities of imagined items. Viola Spolin developed exercises supporting this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick character construction and versatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers must be able to construct characters quickly using physicality, gestures, accents, voice changes, or other techniques, and may be required to play characters of different age or sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character motivations and objectives are important; improvisers should act according to what their character seeks to accomplish. Rapid, clear character choices help other performers accept offers and move scenes forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize character motivations/objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Character motivations are an important part of successful improv scenes; improvisers must attempt to act according to the objectives they believe their character seeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on objectives (what a character wants) gives scenes direction and makes offers meaningful. Objective-driven play ties actions to believable behavior and helps generate conflict and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene structure and transitions in multi-scene formats
rubrics_metrics.description: In improv formats with multiple scenes, an agreed-upon signal is used to denote scene changes (commonly a 'wipe' where a performer runs in front of the scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other transition methods include tapping a character in or out. Performers not in the scene often stand at the side or back of the stage and enter/exit by stepping into or out of center; agreed signals maintain clarity and pacing in multi-scene shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortform vs. longform format conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern improv comedy generally falls into shortform and longform categories: shortform consists of short scenes constructed from a predetermined game/structure driven by audience suggestion; longform creates shows with short scenes interrelated by story, characters, or themes (e.g., the Harold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shortform emphasizes rapid, game-based payoff and audience-friendly bits (popularized by Whose Line Is It Anyway?). Longform emphasizes through-lines, character and thematic development, and structures that allow scenes to echo or interconnect across a show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use audience suggestions and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisational theatre often allows an interactive relationship with the audience; improv groups frequently solicit suggestions from the audience as a source of inspiration and to prove the performance is unscripted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience input can drive premises, games, or scene seeds. Using suggestions effectively demonstrates spontaneity and engages spectators, but performers must still build disciplined offers and acceptances to turn suggestions into coherent scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-rehearsed or apparently scripted scenes (maintain spontaneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because audiences sometimes suspect detailed performances are planned, improvisers should preserve spontaneity so the show appears unscripted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some masters' performances can seem so detailed they appear scripted, authentic improvisation relies on genuine co-creation in present time; training (e.g., theatre games) helps performers generate polished-seeming material without prewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative co-creation and ensemble responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For an improvised scene to be successful, the improvisers involved must work together responsively to define the parameters and action of the scene in a process of co-creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each performer must listen, accept, and build; ensemble awareness and mutual support are prioritized over individual spotlighting. Training centers and troupe schools (Second City, UCB, etc.) emphasize ensemble habits and shared responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of 'gagging' that halts scene progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Gagging is deliberately breaking or blocking for a joke; while it can produce a comic effect, it generally prevents scene advancement and is often discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gagging sparingly and intentionally; prioritize scene development and the group's shared reality unless the ensemble deliberately chooses a gagging style for specific effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational training techniques and theatre games (Viola Spolin, Keith Johnstone, Del Close)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation exercises and theatre games (Spolin, Johnstone, Close) provide techniques for learning, teaching, and structuring improv performance (e.g., theatre games for shortform, Harold for longform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods supply concrete practice drills, structures, and pedagogical sequences; performers and teachers should use established exercises to develop skills like making offers, accepting, endowment, and ensemble play.
